title: Rare Exocrine Pancreatic Malignancies in the United States: A Population-Based Atlas of Epidemiology, Clinical Characteristics, Treatment, and Survival
content: Background/Objectives: Rare exocrine pancreatic malignancies are heterogeneous tumors with pop-ulation evidence fragmented across histologies, coding definitions, calendar eras, and analytic ap-proaches. We developed a classification-aware comparative atlas spanning incidence, phenotype, treatment receipt, and survival. Methods: Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results data through 2023 were analyzed across 20 prespecified histologic groups using entity-specific valid coding eras. Incidence trends used Joinpoint regression for sufficiently stable annual series. Adult treatment re-ceipt was compared with same-era conventional pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma using multivari-able or bias-reduced logistic regression. Survival analyses incorporated proportional-hazards diag-nostics, piecewise Cox models when required, and Firth penalized Cox regression for select ultra-rare comparisons. Results: The clinical atlas included 162,644 cases, including 153,976 conventional pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas. Adenosquamous and acinar cell carcinoma incidence increased, whereas colloid/mucinous and signet-ring carcinoma incidence declined. Broadening the squamous morphology definition increased case count and incidence by approximately 39%, compared with approximately 1% for the expanded acinar family. Treatment receipt varied by histology. Median overall survival ranged from 3.4 months for squamous and undifferentiated carcinomas to not reached for solid pseudopapillary neoplasm. Nine endpoint-histology comparisons showed residual nonproportional hazards, including early excess mortality for signet-ring and undifferentiated carci-nomas and favorable time-varying associations for invasive intraductal papillary mucinous and solid pseudopapillary neoplasms. Conclusions: Rare exocrine pancreatic malignancies differ substantially in epidemiology, treatment patterns, and the temporal structure of mortality. Standardized morphol-ogy definitions and time-aware survival modeling improve population interpretation and support histology-specific investigation rather than uniform extrapolation from conventional pancreatic duc-tal adenocarcinoma.
